tagline: A short follow-up letter to a persecuted church, correcting the claim that the Day of the Lord had already come and calling idle members back to work.
overview:
Second Thessalonians is a brief letter in three chapters, sent in the names of Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy to the same church in Thessalonica that received 1 Thessalonians. The church was still suffering persecution, and something had shaken it badly: a message, whether by a prophetic word, a spoken report, or a letter claiming to come from Paul, that the Day of the Lord had already arrived. Some members, perhaps unsettled by that belief, had stopped working and were living off others.

The letter answers in three movements. Chapter 1 encourages the suffering believers with the promise that God is just: when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven, he will give relief to his afflicted people and bring judgment on those who oppress them. Chapter 2 corrects the false report. The Day of the Lord will not come until a rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness is revealed, a figure who exalts himself against every god and sets himself up in God's temple, but whom the Lord Jesus will destroy at his coming. For now something or someone is restraining him. Chapter 3 asks for prayer and deals firmly but pastorally with those who refuse to work, reminding the church of Paul's own example and of the rule he had taught them: if anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat.

The letter is short, and its central passage (2:1-12) is among the most puzzling in the New Testament. But its main concerns are plain: steadiness under pressure, confidence in God's justice, refusal to be stampeded by end-times claims, and ordinary faithfulness in daily work.
author:
The letter names Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy as senders (1:1), and Paul adds a greeting in his own hand as the mark in every letter (3:17). The early church accepted it as Paul's, and it appears in the earliest lists and collections of his letters.

Its authorship is more debated than that of 1 Thessalonians. Scholars who think a later follower of Paul wrote it point to several features: its structure and wording follow 1 Thessalonians very closely, sometimes phrase for phrase, while its tone is cooler and more formal; its teaching about the end seems to differ, since 1 Thessalonians says the Day will come suddenly like a thief, while 2 Thessalonians lists events that must happen first; and the stress on Paul's signature and the warning against a letter seeming to be from us (2:2) could suggest a later writer claiming Paul's authority against other writings in his name. Scholars who hold that Paul wrote it answer that close similarity is exactly what one would expect in two letters written to the same church within weeks or months; that the change of tone suits a letter correcting a misunderstanding; that Jewish and early Christian teaching, including Jesus' own teaching in Mark 13, holds together both the suddenness of the end and signs that precede it; and that Paul had good reason to guard against forged letters if one had in fact reached the church. A few scholars even argue that 2 Thessalonians was written before 1 Thessalonians. The majority of evangelical and many other scholars accept Paul's authorship; a large part of critical scholarship does not.
date: If Paul wrote it, he wrote it from Corinth soon after 1 Thessalonians, around AD 50 or 51, while Silvanus and Timothy were still with him (Acts 18:5); the two letters would then be only weeks or months apart. Scholars who see it as the work of a later writer usually date it toward the end of the first century, often somewhere between AD 70 and 100. Some have connected the reference to the temple of God (2:4) with the period before the temple's destruction in AD 70, which would favor an earlier date, though others read the temple figuratively.
setting: The setting is the same as for 1 Thessalonians: Thessalonica, the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia and a free city on the Via Egnatia, where Paul founded a mostly Gentile church around AD 49 or 50 (Acts 17:1-10). The believers had faced hostility from the start, and the persecution had continued and perhaps grown (1:4). Some in the church had been told that the Day of the Lord had already come (2:2); what they meant by that is unclear, but it seems to have unsettled them deeply. Some members had also stopped working and were living disorderly lives, depending on others and meddling in their affairs (3:6-12). In a city where many poor people relied on wealthy patrons, and where the church shared meals and resources, this placed a real burden on others and damaged the church's standing.
purpose: The letter aims to encourage the church to persevere under persecution by assuring them of God's just judgment and of their future relief (chapter 1); to correct the false teaching that the Day of the Lord had already come, by reminding them of what Paul had taught about the events that must come first (2:1-12); to strengthen their confidence that God chose and called them (2:13-17); and to direct the church to deal with members who refused to work, withdrawing from them without treating them as enemies (3:6-15).
story: Second Thessalonians continues the conversation begun in 1 Thessalonians and shows a young church working out what it means to wait for the Lord's coming while living an ordinary life. It draws on the prophets' language for the Day of the Lord and on Daniel's visions of a ruler who exalts himself against God and defiles the sanctuary (Daniel 7 to 11), and it anticipates the later New Testament teaching about antichrists (1 John 2:18) and the beast of Revelation 13. Its place in the story is at the church's beginning, but its subject is the story's end.
christ: The Lord Jesus stands at the center of the letter's hope. He will be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, to be glorified in his saints and to judge those who do not know God (1:7-10). He will destroy the lawless one with the breath of his mouth and the majesty of his arrival (2:8), which echoes the messianic king of Isaiah 11:4. As in 1 Thessalonians, he is named with God the Father as the source of grace and peace (1:2) and of comfort and hope (2:16-17), and the letter even places his name first. The glory of Christ is what believers are called to share (2:14).
reading:
Read 2 Thessalonians as a pastoral correction, not an end-times timetable. Its purpose in chapter 2 is to calm a frightened church, not to satisfy curiosity, and Paul assumes the readers already know what he taught them in person (2:5-6), which means we are overhearing half a conversation. Be honest about what cannot be known: the identity of the restrainer, in particular, has puzzled readers since the early centuries, and Augustine admitted he did not know what Paul meant. Watch for the contrast between the lawless one and the Lord Jesus, and between those who refuse the love of the truth and those whom God chose. Don't miss chapter 3, which brings the whole letter down to earth.

The man of lawlessness has been read in several main ways. Many readers, from Irenaeus in the second century to most modern futurist interpreters, take him as a single person who will appear shortly before Christ's return, the figure later called the Antichrist. Others read the passage against Paul's own century, recalling the emperor Caligula's attempt in AD 40 to have his statue set up in the Jerusalem temple, or pointing to Nero or to the events leading to AD 70. Many Protestant Reformers and some later confessions identified the man of sin with the papacy, a reading few hold today. Still others see a recurring power of rebellion against God that takes shape in many rulers and systems through history and will come to a head at the end. Each reading has its strengths, and the chapter note on 2 Thessalonians 2 sets them out more fully.

structure.title: Encouragement in persecution
structure.summary: Paul thanks God for the church's growing faith and love under persecution and assures them that God will judge their oppressors and give them relief at the revelation of the Lord Jesus.

structure.title: The Day of the Lord has not come
structure.summary: The rebellion and the man of lawlessness must come first; the lawless one is now restrained, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him at his coming.

structure.title: Chosen and called
structure.summary: Paul thanks God for choosing the Thessalonians for salvation, urges them to stand firm in the traditions they were taught, and prays for their comfort.

structure.title: Request for prayer
structure.summary: Paul asks for prayer for the spread of the word and for deliverance from wicked people, and expresses confidence in the Lord's faithfulness.

structure.title: Warning against idleness and farewell
structure.summary: The church must withdraw from those who refuse to work, following Paul's example, but treat them as brothers, and receive Paul's signed greeting.

themes.title: God's just judgment
themes.body: The letter insists that God is just and that the suffering of his people is not the end of the story. At the revelation of the Lord Jesus, the persecuted will receive relief and those who oppress them and refuse the gospel will receive judgment (1:5-10). This is offered to encourage the persecuted, not to invite them to take vengeance themselves.

themes.title: The Day of the Lord
themes.body: Against the claim that the Day had already come, Paul teaches that it will be preceded by a rebellion and the revelation of the man of lawlessness. The church is not to be shaken by excited reports but to hold to what it was taught. The letter's teaching about the end is meant to steady, not to alarm.

themes.title: Evil restrained and defeated
themes.body: The mystery of lawlessness is already at work, but it is held back, and when it is finally revealed it will be destroyed by the Lord Jesus at his coming (2:6-8). Evil in this letter is real, deceptive, and powerful, but it is never out of God's control.

themes.title: Chosen for salvation
themes.body: Paul sets God's choice of the Thessalonians for salvation, through the Spirit's sanctifying work and belief in the truth, against the deception of those who are perishing (2:13-14). Election here is offered as reason for thanksgiving and stability.

themes.title: Work and order
themes.body: Waiting for the Lord does not excuse anyone from ordinary work. Paul points to his own labor night and day, reminds the church of his rule that those unwilling to work should not eat, and directs them to deal with the idle firmly but as brothers, not enemies (3:6-15).

keyChapters.why: The promise of relief for the persecuted and judgment on their oppressors at the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven.
The central and much-debated passage on the rebellion, the man of lawlessness, and the restrainer, followed by thanksgiving for God's choice of the church.
Paul's request for prayer and his instructions about members who refuse to work, with the reminder of his own example.
